title: He Delivered Parcels for Australia Post. Now Delhi-Born Nikhil Chaudhary Could End a 62-Year Wait.
excerpt: Stranded by COVID in Brisbane, the former Punjab cricketer rebuilt his career from grade cricket to the Hobart Hurricanes to Australia's T20I squad — and could become the first India-born man to represent Australia since 1964.
body:
He delivered parcels for Australia Post. He flipped burritos at a Mexican restaurant in Brisbane. He played weekend grade cricket while the world was locked down.

On Thursday, Cricket Australia named Nikhil Chaudhary in their T20 International squad for the upcoming series against Bangladesh. If the 30-year-old Delhi-born all-rounder makes the playing XI in Chattogram, he will become the first India-born man to wear Australian colours in white-ball cricket — and the first to represent Australia in any format — since Rex Sellers, a Gujarat-born leg-spinner who played a solitary Test in Kolkata in 1964.

Sixty-two years. That is how long the gap will have been.

## From Punjab Domestic Cricket to COVID Limbo

Chaudhary's cricket story began on Delhi's dusty maidans before he moved through the domestic system, representing Punjab in 14 matches between 2017 and 2019 across the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy, Inter State T20 tournament, and Vijay Hazare Trophy. He shared dressing rooms with future India stars Shubman Gill and Abhishek Sharma. He trialled with Mumbai Indians in the IPL.

But opportunities were sparse. In early 2020, Chaudhary flew to Brisbane to visit his uncle — a short family trip, nothing more. Then COVID-19 sealed Australia's borders. He could not go home.



> **""Nikhil has been a player of national interest for some time," selector Tony Dodemaide said."**


Rather than wait, he chose to rebuild. He found work delivering parcels and at a Mexican restaurant while playing grade cricket in Brisbane — the Australian equivalent of starting over in the gully.

## The Hurricanes and the Breakthrough

Former Hobart Hurricanes bowling coach James Hopes spotted Chaudhary in Brisbane grade cricket and gave him a chance. Chaudhary took it with both hands. He became a regular for Tasmania in the Sheffield Shield, scored a maiden first-class century, and took a five-wicket haul. In the Big Bash League, he was instrumental in the Hurricanes' 2024-25 title run, batting aggressively in the middle order and contributing tight leg-spin.

This IPL season, the Delhi Capitals brought him into their setup — an India-born player, now firmly in the Australian system, invited back to the league where Indian cricket's money and prestige converge.

"Nikhil has been a player of national interest for some time," selector Tony Dodemaide said. "The panel has been impressed by his BBL form, particularly last season. He will gain invaluable experience in Bangladesh and will be in contention to play his first game for Australia when we sit down to pick a team."

## The Diaspora Angle That Writes Itself

Chaudhary's journey mirrors thousands of Indian migrants in Australia who arrived with one plan and stayed to build another. He secured permanent residency — enough to qualify for national selection despite not yet holding citizenship. His path from Delhi to Brisbane to Hobart to a national call-up is a uniquely modern diaspora story: not a child of immigrants raised in the system, but a grown professional who pivoted countries and started again.

For Australia's vast Indian-origin community — now numbering over 900,000 — his selection carries emotional weight. Gurinder Sandhu and Tanveer Sangha have played for Australia as cricketers of Indian heritage, but neither was born in India. On the women's side, Lisa Sthalekar, born in Pune and adopted by Australian parents, carved out a distinguished career. Chaudhary's case is different: he played Ranji Trophy-adjacent cricket, he grew up in the Indian system, and he walked away to build something new.

Travis Head's withdrawal from the Bangladesh tour for personal reasons opened the door. Chaudhary walked through it carrying a very specific kind of baggage — the kind that makes you deliver parcels before lunch and bat in the nets after.

## What Happens Next

The three-match T20I series against Bangladesh begins June 17 in Chattogram, with Mitchell Marsh captaining. Chaudhary is expected to join the squad in Dhaka. Whether he makes the playing XI will depend on conditions and combinations, but Dodemaide's phrasing — "in contention to play" — suggests this is more than a token reward.

If he does debut, the scorecards will show an Australian cricketer born in Delhi on May 4, 1996. The story behind it will show something bigger: that diaspora journeys do not always follow the script, and sometimes the detour is the destination.

*Sources: ESPNcricinfo, Cricket Australia, The Indian Eye, Inside Sport India*
